title: Femoroacetabular Impingement Syndrome and Labral Presentations
case: Case: A 28-year-old recreational footballer has 8 months of right groin pain with deep squats, getting out of the car and kicking. He feels an occasional catch. FADIR reproduces his groin pain. Passive hip flexion and internal rotation are reduced compared with the other side. Hip strength is good. Lumbar and neurological findings are normal. No red flags. An X-ray (ordered by his doctor) shows a cam shape.

Working diagnosis: FAI syndrome (cam-type) with possible labral involvement. Plan: education, activity modification, hip and trunk strengthening, graded return to kicking, reassess in 4 to 6 weeks, and an orthopaedic opinion if he does not improve or develops locking.

differentials.name: Hip osteoarthritis
differentials.key: Older, stiff, reduced internal rotation, X-ray changes

differentials.name: Gluteal tendinopathy
differentials.key: Lateral hip pain, trochanter tenderness, single-leg stance pain

differentials.key: Pain with palpation of the tendon, squeeze test, cough, abdominal wall

differentials.name: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis or Perthes in the young
Snapping hip (iliopsoas or iliotibial band)
differentials.key: Audible or palpable snap with movement

qa: Why is a cam shape on X-ray not enough to diagnose FAI syndrome? Cam shapes are common in people without pain, so the diagnosis also needs matching symptoms and examination findings.

Why is a negative FADIR test more useful than a positive one? It is sensitive but not specific, so a negative result makes an intra-articular problem less likely, while a positive result can come from many hip problems.
Why avoid stretching into flexion and internal rotation? That is the position where the shapes meet, so stretching there may irritate the joint.
A 14-year-old has knee pain and a limp with painful hip rotation. What do you do? Treat it as urgent and refer for slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

When do you refer for surgery? After a reasonable trial of rehabilitation without improvement, a true mechanical block, or when function goals cannot be met, with the decision made with the surgeon [Ref - to verify].

tests.name: FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) impingement test

fields.Purpose: Move the hip into a position where a cam or pincer shape and the labrum are most likely to be loaded
fields.Therapist position: Beside the hip; one hand on the knee and the other on the ankle or foot
fields.Action: Flex the hip to about 90 degrees, then adduct and internally rotate it by moving the foot outward; stop at the first pain or at end range
fields.Positive: Reproduction of the familiar groin or hip pain, sometimes with a block to movement or a click
fields.Supports: A positive test supports an intra-articular hip problem such as FAI, labral injury or OA
fields.Limits: Low specificity; a negative result makes an intra-articular problem less likely but does not exclude it [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Moving too fast; forcing end range; counting a stretch feeling or buttock pain as positive
fields.Next step: Check range, other tests and imaging need

fields.Action: Measure passive hip flexion and internal rotation with a goniometer or inclinometer, and compare with the other side
fields.Positive: Reduced flexion or internal rotation, especially with pain at the end of range, supports FAI-type restriction
fields.Limits: Normal values differ between people, and range may be reduced because of pain or muscle guarding [Ref - to verify]

fields.Purpose: Check for pain from hip joint structures with minimal muscle loading
fields.Position: Supine with legs straight and relaxed
fields.Action: Roll the whole leg inward and outward by holding the thigh or lower leg
fields.Positive: Groin pain or a click; a firm block

fields.Action: The patient lifts the straight leg to about 30 degrees against resistance
fields.Supports: Hip joint or iliopsoas involvement; not specific

redFlags.Finding: Adolescent with a limp and limited or painful hip rotation
Pain with impact, runner or low bone density
After a fall: cannot bear weight, shortened externally rotated leg
Constant night pain, weight loss, cancer history
Sudden severe pain with steroid use, alcohol or sickle cell disease
Locked hip with a true mechanical block
redFlags.Why it matters: Loose body or large labral tear

redFlags.Finding: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change

manual.name: Hip joint mobilization (gentle long-axis distraction or lateral glides)
manual.why: Short-term pain relief in some patients
manual.stop: Pain increases or a catch develops

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education, activity modification and exercise therapy. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not use techniques that force the hip into the impingement position. Avoid repeated end-range flexion and internal rotation stretching. Do not claim that manual therapy reshapes the bone or repairs the labrum.

exercise.Exercises: Pain-free range, walking, cycling with a higher seat, relative rest from deep flexion and twisting
Bridge, side-lying abduction, clam, hip hinge, sit-to-stand to a higher chair, trunk stability (dead bug, side plank)
Step-up, split squat, single-leg squat, Romanian deadlift, controlled squat to a pain-free depth
exercise.Progress when: Control, no catch or groin pain

exercise.Exercises: Running progression, change of direction, sport drills

exerciseNotes: Principle: a supervised, progressive program of hip and trunk strengthening, movement control and activity modification is a first-line option. Trials comparing physiotherapy with hip arthroscopy show improvement in both groups, with arthroscopy giving larger gains in pain and function at about 12 months in some trials [Ref - to verify]. The choice depends on the patient's goals, the severity, a sport or work demand and the response to rehabilitation, and is made with the orthopaedic surgeon.

Activity modification: avoid deep squats, low seats, sitting with the knees above the hips for long periods, and repeated pivoting under load early on. Shorten stride, add cushioned shoes and adjust bike seat height as needed. Aim to reduce, not remove, activity.
Symptom rule: pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within 24 hours is acceptable. Sharp pain, catching or locking means stop and reassess.

Return to sport criteria (example): pain-free daily activity, near-normal strength compared with the other side, good single-leg control, and tolerance of sport drills with no catch or groin pain. If surgery is performed, follow the surgeon's protocol, which usually limits range and weight-bearing at first [Ref - to verify].
modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): anti-inflammatory medicines, intra-articular injections for pain relief or for diagnostic purposes, and hip arthroscopy for selected patients with FAI syndrome who do not improve with rehabilitation or who have a mechanical block [Ref - to verify].
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.

Motion- or position-related groin or front hip pain, a positive FADIR test and other signs, reduced flexion or internal rotation, and no other cause? Yes: working diagnosis is suspected FAI syndrome. Confirmation requires imaging findings of a cam or pincer shape by a doctor.
Catching or locking and positive provocation tests? Suspect a labral tear and arrange medical review if it persists.
Begin education, activity modification and exercise therapy.
If there is no improvement after a good trial or if there is a mechanical block, discuss specialist review, including arthroscopic options [Ref - to verify].
Visit 1: screen flags (especially in adolescents), examine, explain FAI as a shape-and-load condition, discuss activity changes.
Early: reduce impingement positions, begin pain-free strength and control.
Middle: progress strength, functional movement and sport-specific drills.
